questions.stem: What is stratification in a community?
options: Vertical layering, such as canopy, shrub and ground layers in a forest
Horizontal banding of species along a gradient, such as up a rocky shore
The gradual change in species over time after a disturbance
The movement of nutrients between living and non-living parts
questions.explanation: Stratification is the vertical layering of a community, as in a forest with an emergent and canopy layer, a shrub layer and a ground layer. Horizontal banding along an environmental gradient is zonation.

questions.stem: Walking from the beach inland, a student passes bands of different plants: spinifex grass on the foredune, then low shrubs, then coastal woodland. Which pattern is this?
options: A food chain from producers to top consumers
Zonation along a gradient of abiotic conditions
Stratification into vertical layers of vegetation
Secondary succession after a recent bushfire
questions.explanation: Zonation is the arrangement of species in bands across an area as abiotic conditions such as salt spray, wind and soil change. Stratification describes vertical layers at one place.

questions.stem: In a tall forest, light at the forest floor is about 2% of that above the canopy. Which feature would you expect in plants of the ground layer?
options: Small, thick leaves with sunken stomata to reduce water loss
No chlorophyll, because they get all their energy from the soil
Leaves held edge-on to the sun to avoid overheating at midday
Large, thin leaves that capture as much dim light as possible
questions.explanation: Light decreases sharply down through the layers of a stratified forest, so ground-layer plants tend to have large, thin leaves suited to capturing dim light. Small, thick leaves and edge-on leaves suit bright, hot, dry conditions.

questions.stem: How does energy enter most ecosystems?
options: Decomposers release energy from dead organisms
Consumers absorb heat energy from their surroundings
Water carries chemical energy into the soil
Producers capture light energy in photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Most ecosystems are powered by sunlight, which producers capture and transform into chemical energy in organic molecules by photosynthesis. This energy then passes to consumers and decomposers through feeding.

questions.stem: Producers in a grassland capture 50 000 kJ of energy per square metre per year. If about 10% passes to each trophic level, how much reaches the secondary consumers?
options: 50 kJ
5 kJ
500 kJ
questions.explanation: About 10% of 50 000 kJ reaches primary consumers, giving 5000 kJ, and about 10% of that reaches secondary consumers, giving 500 kJ. Stopping after one step gives 5000 kJ, which is the energy for primary consumers.

questions.stem: Why is only a small fraction of the energy in one trophic level passed to the next?
options: Energy is recycled back to the producers before it is able to reach the consumers
Consumers convert most of the energy they eat into new chemical elements
Producers store all their energy as starch, which no consumer can digest
Much is lost as heat from respiration or remains in uneaten and undigested parts
questions.explanation: At each level, organisms use much of their energy in respiration, which is released as heat, and some material is not eaten or is lost in faeces. Energy is not recycled; it flows through and leaves the ecosystem as heat.

questions.stem: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
options: Too little energy remains at higher levels to support another population
Top predators would eat all of the producers if the chains were any longer
Nutrients such as nitrogen cannot be recycled past the fourth level
Decomposers break down all animals that are above the fourth level
questions.explanation: Because roughly 90% of the energy is lost at each step, very little energy is left after four or five levels, too little to sustain a population of another predator. Nutrient recycling is not limited by trophic level.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how energy and matter move through ecosystems?
options: Both energy and matter are lost permanently at each trophic level
Energy flows through and is lost as heat; matter is recycled
Energy is recycled by decomposers; matter flows through and is lost
Both energy and matter are recycled by decomposers indefinitely
questions.explanation: Energy enters as light and leaves as heat, so it must be continually supplied. Chemical elements such as carbon and nitrogen are recycled between living things and the non-living environment in biogeochemical cycles.

questions.stem: Which process in the water cycle releases water vapour from plant leaves?
options: Transpiration
Condensation
Precipitation
Infiltration
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plants, mainly through stomata. Condensation forms clouds, precipitation returns water as rain, and infiltration is water soaking into the soil.

questions.stem: Large areas of forest are cleared for farming. How is the local water cycle most likely to change?
options: More transpiration and less surface runoff
More infiltration and less evaporation from soil
No change, because trees do not affect the cycle
Less transpiration and more surface runoff
questions.explanation: Trees return large amounts of water to the air by transpiration and slow rainfall so it soaks in. Removing them reduces transpiration and increases runoff, which can also increase erosion.

questions.stem: In the carbon cycle, which process takes carbon dioxide out of the air and fixes it in organic molecules?
options: Combustion
Decomposition
Photosynthesis
Respiration
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and fixes the carbon into organic molecules. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all release carbon dioxide back to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Coal formed from plants buried hundreds of millions of years ago. What does burning it do to the carbon cycle?
options: It returns long-stored carbon to the air, raising carbon dioxide levels
It removes carbon dioxide from the air and stores it in rocks underground
It converts atmospheric carbon dioxide into oxygen through combustion
It has no effect, because the carbon released was already in the air
questions.explanation: Coal, oil and gas formed from organisms buried long ago, locking carbon away from the cycle. Burning them returns that carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide much faster than natural processes remove it.

questions.stem: Seawater absorbs some of the extra carbon dioxide released by human activity. What is a consequence for marine organisms?
options: The pH of seawater rises, making shells and coral skeletons grow faster
The water becomes less salty, so fish lose water to the sea by osmosis
Phytoplankton stop photosynthesising because carbon dioxide is toxic to them
The pH of seawater falls, making it harder to build calcium carbonate shells
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolving in seawater forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH (ocean acidification). This reduces the carbonate available to organisms such as corals and molluscs that build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.

questions.stem: Which organisms convert nitrogen gas from the air into compounds that plants can use?
options: Decomposing fungi
Grazing herbivores
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria
Denitrifying bacteria
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, some free-living in soil and some in the root nodules of legumes, convert nitrogen gas into ammonium. Denitrifying bacteria do the opposite, returning nitrogen gas to the air.

questions.stem: Farmers often grow legumes such as clover or lupins before a wheat crop. Why does this improve the soil?
options: Bacteria in legume root nodules fix nitrogen, adding nitrogen compounds
Legumes absorb nitrogen gas through their leaves and store it as starch
Legumes release phosphorus gas from their roots into the soil air
Legumes kill the denitrifying bacteria that make nitrate in soil
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium, which the plant uses. When the legume dies and decomposes, these nitrogen compounds enrich the soil for the next crop.

questions.stem: A paddock becomes waterlogged for several weeks and the soil has little oxygen. Which change to the nitrogen cycle is most likely?
options: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria release more oxygen into the soil
Plants absorb more nitrogen gas directly through their roots
Denitrifying bacteria convert more nitrate to nitrogen gas
Nitrifying bacteria convert more ammonium to nitrate
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria thrive in anaerobic, waterlogged soils and convert nitrate into nitrogen gas, so soil nitrogen is lost. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so nitrification slows in these conditions.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows nitrogen moving from a dead animal to a plant?
options: Protein -> nitrate -> nitrogen gas -> ammonium -> plant protein
Protein -> nitrogen gas -> nitrite -> ammonium -> plant protein
Protein -> nitrite -> nitrogen gas -> nitrate -> plant protein
Protein -> ammonium -> nitrite -> nitrate -> plant protein
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down protein, releasing ammonium. Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate, which plant roots absorb and use to make proteins. Nitrogen gas is not part of this pathway.

questions.stem: How does the phosphorus cycle differ from the carbon and nitrogen cycles?
options: It has no significant gas phase in the atmosphere
It does not involve living organisms at any stage
It moves only through the oceans, not through the land
It depends on lightning to make phosphorus usable
questions.explanation: Phosphorus cycles mainly through rocks, soil, water and organisms. It is released by the weathering of rocks, taken up by plants as phosphate and returned by decomposition, with no important atmospheric form.

questions.stem: Phosphate fertiliser is made by mining phosphate rock. Why is this a concern for the long-term phosphorus supply?
options: Rock phosphate forms over geological time, much more slowly than it is mined
Mined phosphate escapes into the atmosphere as a gas and is lost permanently
Phosphorus in fertiliser is converted into nitrogen by the soil bacteria
Plants cannot use phosphate from fertiliser, only phosphate from rainfall
questions.explanation: New phosphate rock forms from sediments over millions of years, so mining is removing it far faster than it is replaced. Phosphorus washed from farms ends up in waterways and ocean sediments, where it is not readily available.

questions.stem: What does an organism's ecological niche describe?
options: Its position in the classification system of living things
The number of individuals of its species in an ecosystem
Its habitat, feeding relationships and interactions with other species
Only the physical place where it lives and shelters within its ecosystem
questions.explanation: A niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem: where it lives, what it eats and what eats it, and how it interacts with other species and abiotic conditions. The habitat is only one part of the niche.

questions.stem: Two bird species live in the same woodland. One feeds on insects in the canopy, and the other feeds on insects on the ground. Why can both persist?
options: They live in different habitats in different regions
Their niches are the same, but one will soon go extinct
Their niches differ, so they compete less for food
They share an identical niche, so they cooperate
questions.explanation: Feeding in different layers of the woodland means their niches overlap only partly, reducing competition. Two species with identical niches in the same place would be expected to compete until one is excluded.

questions.stem: Which statement defines a keystone species?
options: Any species that is listed as endangered in an ecosystem
A species that is found only in a single small area
A species with a much larger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers suggest
The most abundant species of producer found anywhere in an ecosystem
questions.explanation: A keystone species plays a critical role in maintaining the structure of its ecosystem, often far beyond what its abundance would suggest. Removing it can cause major changes to the community.

questions.stem: Along parts of the North American Pacific coast, sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze kelp. Where sea otters were hunted out, kelp forests largely disappeared. What does this show?
options: Sea otters are a keystone species that maintains the kelp community
Sea urchins are producers, so their numbers set the size of the kelp forest
Kelp is a keystone species because it was the most abundant species
Sea otters compete with kelp for light, so removing them harmed kelp
questions.explanation: By keeping sea urchin numbers low, otters allow kelp forests, and the many species that live in them, to persist. The large effect of removing one predator identifies it as a keystone species.

questions.stem: Why would a sharp decline in a keystone species concern conservation managers?
options: The ecosystem would gain biodiversity as new species replace the keystone
Producers would no longer be able to carry out photosynthesis at all
Many other species could decline because the ecosystem's structure would change
Only that species would be affected, because each species occupies its own niche
questions.explanation: Because keystone species have large effects on other species, losing them can trigger cascading changes and losses of biodiversity. This is why such species can be a priority for protection.

questions.stem: What is ecological succession?
options: The gradual change in the species of a community over time
The movement of energy from one trophic level to the next
The arrangement of species in vertical layers in a forest
The process by which bacteria fix nitrogen from the air
questions.explanation: Succession is a sequence of changes in a community over time, in which biotic and abiotic components influence each other. Early species change conditions, allowing other species to establish.

questions.stem: Which situation is an example of primary rather than secondary succession?
options: Weeds growing on a cleared building site with intact soil
Lichens and mosses colonising bare rock left by a retreating glacier
Grasses regrowing in a paddock that was ploughed and then abandoned
Eucalypt seedlings appearing in a forest after a bushfire
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts on newly exposed surfaces with no soil, such as bare rock or new lava. When soil remains after a disturbance, as after fire or ploughing, the change is secondary succession.

questions.stem: During succession on bare rock, lichens grow first, followed by mosses, then grasses and later shrubs. How do the lichens make it possible for later species to establish?
options: They produce seeds that grow into the mosses and grasses that follow
They remove all nutrients from the rock so that only grasses survive
They help break down rock and add organic matter, starting soil formation
They shade out all of the other species so that only shrubs are able to grow later
questions.explanation: Pioneer species such as lichens release acids that weather rock, trap particles, and add organic matter when they die, beginning soil formation. Changed abiotic conditions then allow other species to establish.

questions.stem: Fossils of marine shellfish are found in rock layers in the middle of a continent, far from the sea. What can be inferred?
options: The rocks formed in a desert that later became wetter
The area was once covered by sea when those rocks formed
The shellfish were carried there recently by birds or people
The shellfish evolved to live on land after the sea receded
questions.explanation: Fossils record the organisms living where sediments were deposited. Marine fossils show the environment was once a sea, giving evidence of long-term environmental change.

questions.stem: A sediment core from a lake bed contains pollen. The deepest layers are dominated by rainforest tree pollen, while upper layers are mainly eucalypt and grass pollen. What does this suggest?
options: The lake was formed after all the rainforest trees had grown there
The surrounding vegetation changed from rainforest to drier woodland over time
Rainforest trees grew in the area more recently than the eucalypts and grasses did
Pollen from eucalypts sinks faster than rainforest pollen in water
questions.explanation: Deeper layers are older, so the change in pollen from bottom to top records vegetation changing from rainforest to woodland and grassland, probably as the climate became drier or fire became more frequent. Geological deposits like this provide evidence of long-term change.

questions.stem: How does clearing native vegetation for farmland reduce biodiversity?
options: The cleared land gains more species, because more light reaches the soil
Only producers are affected, because animals simply move to new areas
Species lose habitat, food and shelter, and remaining patches become isolated
Native species quickly adapt to the new crops and so increase greatly in number
questions.explanation: Habitat destruction removes the food, shelter and breeding sites that species need, and leaves small, isolated patches that support fewer species. This speeds up ecosystem change far beyond natural rates.

questions.stem: Monitoring shows that atmospheric carbon dioxide has risen by about 2.5 ppm per year for the past decade, to 410 ppm. If this trend continues, what is the predicted level 10 years later?
options: 460 ppm
4100 ppm
435 ppm
questions.explanation: Extrapolating the trend: 2.5 ppm per year x 10 years = 25 ppm, and 410 + 25 = 435 ppm. Extrapolation assumes the trend continues, which is a limitation of any such prediction.

questions.stem: Sea temperature records for a coral reef show summer maxima rising over several decades. How can measurements like these help reduce harm to the reef?
options: They prove exactly which year every coral on the reef will die
They show that sea temperature has no effect, so all reef management can stop now
They replace the need to monitor any living organisms on the reef
They allow predictions of future bleaching, guiding strategies to protect the reef
questions.explanation: Measuring key abiotic and biotic components over time reveals trends that can be used to predict impacts, such as coral bleaching in hotter summers. These predictions help managers plan strategies, although they cannot give exact certainty.

questions.stem: Why is extrapolating a graph of a species' declining population over the next 30 years less reliable than interpolating within the measured years?
options: It uses fewer data points than interpolation always does
It can only be done for abiotic factors, not for populations
It requires the population to have been counted every day
It assumes the trend will continue, though conditions may change
questions.explanation: Extrapolation extends a trend beyond the measured range, assuming conditions stay the same. New threats or conservation action could change the trend, so predictions further into the future are more uncertain.

questions.stem: Fertiliser runoff adds nitrate and phosphate to a river that flows into a bay. Which change to the bay's ecosystem is most likely?
options: Algal growth decreases because added nutrients are toxic to most species of algae
Fish numbers increase because nitrate is a source of oxygen
Seagrass grows faster because algae on its leaves are removed
Algal blooms increase, then oxygen falls as the algae decompose
questions.explanation: Extra nitrate and phosphate cause rapid algal growth (eutrophication). When the algae die, decomposers use up dissolved oxygen, which can kill fish. Algae can also shade seagrass, so seagrass tends to decline.

questions.stem: Why does a population with low genetic diversity face a higher risk of extinction?
options: Every individual will be immune to all of the diseases found in its environment
Low genetic diversity always causes the population to grow too fast
Low genetic diversity means individuals cannot reproduce sexually
Fewer individuals may carry alleles that help them survive a new threat
questions.explanation: With little genetic variation, it is less likely that some individuals carry alleles allowing them to survive a change such as a new disease or a hotter climate. A diverse gene pool gives a better chance that some survive and reproduce.

questions.stem: A population of a small marsupial falls to about 30 individuals after habitat loss, then recovers to several hundred. Why may it still be at risk?
options: The recovered population descends from few survivors, so genetic diversity stays low
The recovered population has more genetic diversity than before the decline
A population of several hundred is too large for any disease to spread through
Breeding among a few survivors always removes all of the harmful alleles from a population
questions.explanation: A population bottleneck reduces genetic diversity because the survivors carry only some of the original alleles, and recovery in numbers does not restore them. Inbreeding can also increase the frequency of harmful recessive alleles.

questions.stem: Which conservation strategy most directly increases the genetic diversity of a small, isolated population?
options: Breeding only the closely related individuals already in the area
Removing all predators so that every individual survives
Introducing individuals from another population of the same species
Fencing the population so that no individuals are able to enter or leave the area
questions.explanation: Bringing in individuals from another population adds new alleles to the gene pool (genetic rescue). Fencing and breeding only close relatives keep diversity low, and removing predators increases numbers but not diversity.

questions.stem: What is the main reason species become extinct at faster rates when humans destroy habitat?
options: Habitat destruction makes organisms evolve resistance to all diseases
Populations lose the resources they need and become small and isolated
Habitat destruction causes every species to mutate into a new species
Habitat destruction adds new resources that attract too many predators
questions.explanation: Destroying habitat removes food, shelter and breeding sites, so populations shrink and become isolated. Small, isolated populations lose genetic diversity and are vulnerable to chance events, increasing extinction risk.
